title: The Lord Is My Shepherd… But Not the Way You’ve Been Told
paragraphs:
The Lord Is My Shepherd… But Not the Way You’ve Been Told
The Psalm that comforts millions—yet confronts the parts of you still hiding from God
You’ve heard it at funerals. Whispered in hospital rooms. Quoted in captions when life feels heavy.
“The Lord is my shepherd…”
It sounds soft. Peaceful. Almost like a lullaby for anxious souls.
But if you really understood what David meant when he wrote it, it wouldn’t just comfort you…
…it would expose you.
Because the truth is, most people love the promise of Psalm 23—but resist the reality of having a Shepherd.
David didn’t write poetry from comfort. He wrote from collision. From failure. From scandal. From nights where guilt didn’t let him sleep and mornings where mercy somehow still found him.

And when he said, in Hebrew,
יְהוָה רֹעִי לֹא אֶחְסָר (Adonai ro’i lo echsar)
“The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not lack”…
he wasn’t saying, “God gives me everything I want.”
He was saying, “I belong to Someone who won’t let me destroy myself anymore.”
That word ro’i—“my shepherd”—is not gentle in the way modern culture imagines.
A shepherd doesn’t just cuddle sheep.

He leads them… even when they resist.
He corrects them… even when they wander.
He disciplines them… when their wandering could cost them their life.
And sheep?
They are not strong. Not independent. Not self-sufficient.
They are dependent.
Completely.
That’s where this hits harder than you expected.

Because many people want God as a provider… but not as an authority.
They want comfort… but not correction.
They want green pastures… but not the rod and the staff.
But David continues:
“He makes me lie down in green pastures…”
That word “makes” in Hebrew carries weight. It implies force, intervention, even interruption.
Because sheep don’t lie down peacefully unless everything is right—no fear, no hunger, no tension.
And sometimes, God has to remove what you keep chasing… just so your soul can finally rest.
You called it loss.
He called it rescue.
“He restores my soul…”
The Hebrew word here, יְשׁוֹבֵב (yeshovev), means “to bring back,” “to return,” “to restore what has wandered.”
This is not maintenance.
This is recovery.
This is God going after the version of you that got lost in sin, in compromise, in exhaustion, in pretending you were okay when you weren’t.
This is not a distant God.
This is a pursuing Shepherd.
And here’s where it gets uncomfortable again:
“He leads me in paths of righteousness for His name’s sake.”
Not for your reputation.
Not for your image.
For His name.
Which means sometimes the path He leads you on will cost you things you were trying to hold onto.
Relationships.
Habits.
Secrets.
Versions of yourself you’ve been protecting.
And then David says something that most people skip over too quickly:
“Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death…”
Notice—through, not around.
The Shepherd doesn’t always remove the valley.
He walks you through it.
The Hebrew phrase גֵּיא צַלְמָוֶת (gei tsalmavet) implies deep darkness, a place where death casts a shadow so real it feels alive.
You’ve been there.

Where anxiety feels louder than truth.
Where guilt whispers your past like it’s your identity.
Where silence feels like abandonment.
But David doesn’t say, “I fear no evil because I’m strong.”
He says, “I fear no evil because You are with me.”
Not explanations.
Presence.
Not answers.
Presence.
Not instant escape.
Presence.
That’s what changes everything.
“Your rod and your staff, they comfort me.”
That sounds strange, doesn’t it?
Because the rod corrects.
The staff guides.
And yet both bring comfort.
Why?
Because they mean you’re not alone.
Because they mean you’re not left to wander into destruction.
Because they mean someone is actually watching over your soul.
And here’s the part most people misunderstand completely:
“You prepare a table before me in the presence of my enemies…”
This is not about flexing on people who doubted you.
This is about peace that exists even when the battle isn’t over.
It’s about sitting in grace while everything around you still looks unresolved.
It’s about God saying, “You don’t have to win every fight… you just have to stay with Me.”
Then David says:
“My cup overflows.”
Not because life is perfect.
But because God is present.
Because grace is real.
Because mercy didn’t run out when you messed up again.
Because the Shepherd didn’t leave when you thought He should.
And then the final line…
“Surely goodness and mercy shall follow me all the days of my life…”
The Hebrew word for “follow,” יִרְדְּפוּנִי (yirdefuni), doesn’t mean gently trail behind.
It means pursue.
Chase.
Run after.
God’s goodness and mercy are not passive.
They are relentless.
They are chasing you… even when you’ve been running the other way.
And this is where everything shifts.
Because “The Lord is my Shepherd” is not a cute verse to memorize.
It is a surrender to live.
It is saying:
“I am no longer leading myself.”
“I am no longer trusting my own broken instincts.”
“I am no longer pretending I don’t need help.”
It is laying down your pride… your control… your illusion of independence…
…and finally letting Jesus lead.
The same Shepherd David wrote about is revealed fully in Christ.
Jesus said in Greek:

ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ ποιμὴν ὁ καλός (egō eimi ho poimēn ho kalos)
“I am the good shepherd.” (John 10:11)
And then He proved it.
“The good shepherd lays down His life for the sheep.”
This is where Psalm 23 stops being poetry…
…and becomes personal.
Because the Shepherd didn’t just guide you.
He died for you.
He stepped into your valley.
He carried your sin.
He took your punishment.
And then He rose—so you could finally come home.
Be honest.
Let someone see your honesty. Let someone stand with you.
And if you feel something pulling you deeper—don’t ignore it.
Following isn’t just clicking a button.
It’s choosing to stay close to truth when everything else feels loud.
If this message reached you, imagine how many more it needs to reach through you.
Because glorifying God isn’t passive.
It’s participation.
It’s obedience.
It’s letting your life—and even your share button—be used for His purpose.
The Shepherd is not just comforting you…
He’s calling you.
And deep down, you know it.
You were never meant to lead your own life.
